metadata.title: Teacher support for student learning: Insights from PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses PISA 2022 microdata covering 15-year-old students across 81 countries and economies, with analyses conducted primarily at the country/economy level and also across time (2003–2022). For school-level reporting, the principals’ questionnaire responses are explicitly weighted to be proportional to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in each school. The paper does not describe the specific student weight variable name(s) (e.g., W_FSTUWT) nor any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), but it relies on PISA’s standard complex survey estimation framework and reports statistically significant differences with confidence intervals. No machine-learning model training is described; therefore, the report’s weighting discussion is about PISA estimation and representativeness rather than ML-specific weight omission.

Teacher support index (TEACHSUP) in mathematics lessons: teacher shows an interest in every student's learning; teacher gives extra help when students need it; teacher helps students with their learning; teacher continues teaching until students understand
data.outcome_summary: This OECD policy paper uses PISA 2022 (and trend data from 2003–2022) to describe teacher support in mathematics lessons and its associations with student outcomes. Students reporting higher teacher support (TEACHSUP) show higher mathematics performance, lower mathematics anxiety, and greater motivation to learn new things, with these relationships reported as holding after accounting for students’ and schools’ socio-economic profiles (ESCS). Teacher support practices follow an inverted-U pattern over time: rising from 2003 to 2012 and declining between 2012 and 2022, with one practice (“the teacher helps students with their learning”) remaining stable from 2003 to 2012. Within-school variation dominates: only about 6% of teacher-support variation occurs between schools (94% within schools). In the school learning environment analysis, the strongest predictor of teacher support is the quality of student-teacher relationships (a one-unit increase associated with a 0.37 increase in the teacher-support index), with disciplinary climate and student persistence also associated but more modestly; the paper explicitly notes these are correlational rather than causal findings.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD PISA policy/report synthesis rather than an empirical ML study. The manuscript does not report an analytic sample size (total N) or per-country student counts, and it does not specify any machine-learning algorithms or model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE). Consequently, ML-related fields are left empty and the extraction focuses on PISA-defined indices and correlational regression-based associations described in the text.
